name: Solrath Dune
geological_features: Continent-sized sand seas with dune formations reaching 800 meters in height
Ancient dried seabeds exposing layered sedimentary formations
Deep sandstone canyon networks carved by long-vanished rivers
specific_features: Thermal burrowers — large fauna that migrate vertically through sand layers following temperature gradients
The Glass Meridian — a 6,000-km band of natural glass formed by ancient lightning storms in silica-rich dunes
Oasis cavern systems where subterranean aquifers support dense pockets of life
description: Solrath Dune is a scorched world of endless sand seas and towering dune formations, where daytime temperatures at the equator can exceed seventy degrees Celsius and the horizon shimmers with heat distortion from dawn to dusk. The planet retains a breathable atmosphere despite its aridity, a relic of a wetter epoch when oceans covered much of the surface. The dried seabeds now form vast flat expanses of cracked sediment between the dune fields.

The air is dry and carries a fine mineral dust that coats everything in a pale ochre film. At night, temperatures plummet rapidly, and the cooling sand produces a deep, resonant groaning that echoes across the dune seas like the breathing of something enormous. The Glass Meridian catches starlight and reflects it in long, sinuous bands that are visible from orbit.

Life on Solrath Dune has adapted to the extremes with remarkable ingenuity. The thermal burrowers — armored creatures ranging from dog-sized to nearly ten meters in length — navigate the sand like fish in water, following thermal gradients to maintain optimal body temperatures. The oasis cavern systems support entire ecosystems in cool, humid darkness, connected by underground waterways that the fauna have learned to navigate across hundreds of kilometers.

Xenozoologists consider Solrath Dune a masterclass in extremophile adaptation, and the planet draws researchers from across the sector. The fauna's heat-resistance mechanisms have potential applications in thermal engineering and biotechnology, though capturing live specimens has proven extraordinarily difficult — the thermal burrowers can sense vibrations through sand at distances exceeding five kilometers and vanish long before any expedition gets close.
